newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major makes friends with poor immigrants.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major makes friends with poor immigrants.

text.p: Embattled John Major found himself among almost too exuberant friends from one of Britain's poorest immigrant communities on Friday as he continued his campaign for re-election as prime minister on May 1.

"Long live John Major, long live the Conservative Party," Bangladeshis living in the east end of London chanted as they mobbed Major when his "battlebus" stopped outside a mosque in the Whitechapel district.
But while Major glad-handed the crowd -- later declaring: "I love it. This is what politics is all about" -- his wife Norma and 72-year-old parliamentary aide John Ward were less enthusiastic.
Mrs Major quickly retreated to the bus to escape being crushed in the crowd surrounding her husband while Ward had to be hustled back on board by concerned party workers.
The mosque is in the constituency of Bethnal Green and Bow, where the Conservatives ran a poor third at the 1992 election.
Major's visit came hours before an election broadcast was screened on British television on behalf of the British National Party, an extreme right-wing anti-immigrant grouping.
Conservatives are hopeful that Bethnal Green and Bow will buck the opinion polls which show slumping support for them nationally.
Their local candidate, Kabir Choudhury, is a Bangladeshi with impeccable credentials in a seat in which 28 percent of electors come from Bangladesh.
He was a member of the steering committee for the Independence Struggle of Bangladesh from Pakistan in the 1970s, and five years ago helped to found the Bangladesh-British Chamber of Commerce.

By contrast, Labour chose Oona King, a woman with a black American father from Georgia and a white Jewish mother, after the national party imposed a shortlist of possible candidates on a reluctant local Labour association.
"Some local people have resigned from the Labour Party, others are coming over to us," said a Conservative official.
"People are very unhappy about the way it (the candidate selection) has been dealt with by Walworth Road (Labour headquarters)".
While a few Labour supporters joined the crowd outside the mosque, their taunts were drowned out by the cries of support for Major.

An hour later, when Major's bus stopped in the east London suburb of Ilford, the scene was very different. Polite applause and muted boos were the order of the day among a much more respectful, mainly white, crowd.
For cricket-loving Major, it must have seemed like a return to the somnolent atmosphere of London's hallowed Lord's from the firecrackers and fanaticism of Calcutta's Eden Gardens.
